extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and advanced students learning scientific method / hypothesis formation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to invent, judge, and test scientific hypotheses: what makes a hypothesis probable or acceptable, how hypotheses should guide experiment, and what defects (vagueness, contradiction, inconsistency with established laws) to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement with observed facts (primary test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement with fact is the sole and sufficient test of a true hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ultimate test of any hypothesis is that it enables us to infer phenomena which occur in experience. A hypothesis must be judged by whether its consequences match observations; this is the single condition from which subordinate conditions follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of deductive reasoning / testable consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A good hypothesis must allow of the application of deductive reasoning and the inference of consequences capable of comparison with the results of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses must be sufficiently definite and conformable to experience to permit deduction of consequences (e.g., mathematical exactness to calculate relations). If you cannot deduce specific, testable consequences, you cannot decide whether the hypothesis holds. Example: the vortex theory failed because it did not allow precise calculation of planetary distances/periods; Newton's theory was subjected to rigorous deductive testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with known laws (no conflict with established truths)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis should not conflict with laws of nature or of mind which we hold to be true; it must not be self-contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a new hypothesis contradicts well-established laws, the onus is on the new hypothesis to disprove those established results before being accepted. A hypothesis that implies logical self-contradiction or contradiction with proven physical laws is 'self-condemned.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences must agree with facts of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The consequences inferred from the hypothesis must agree with observed facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when deductions are possible, they must be compared with fresh observations. Agreement in one case is not final confirmation; the hypothesis must be subjected to multiple further deductions and trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness and mathematical exactness (precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis should possess definiteness and, where appropriate, mathematical exactness to allow precise calculation and comparison with observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vagueness prevents rigorous testing and often allows false theories to survive. Theories that permit precise numerical predictions (e.g., Newton's gravity) can be subjected to severe tests, whereas vague hypotheses (e.g., some vortex theories) cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not self-contradictory (logical coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis must not involve self-contradiction or be inconsistent with the primary laws of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While hypotheses may propose ideas hard to conceive (e.g., instantaneous distant action), they must not break logical consistency. If a hypothesis is self-contradictory, deductive reasoning cannot be applied and it will fail to agree with facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformable to experience or analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses should be 'not fictions altogether arbitrary, but suppositions conformable to experience or analogy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invented causes must be likened to known causes so we can reason about them (e.g., modelling ether by analogy with elastic media). Every worthy hypothesis must suggest some likeness or common law acting in two or more things, enabling deductive inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must guide selection of critical experiments (predictive/heuristic value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses should enable the investigator to anticipate phenomena and to select critical experiments suitable for confirming or negating the hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction consists in marrying hypothesis and experiment: theory must lead us to choose the critical experiments out of the infinite possibilities (seek singular/exceptional phenomena that would follow if the hypothesis were true). Even passive observation is improved when guided by theoretical anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the accumulated body of science to form and judge hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: In framing and testing hypotheses, the investigator should avail himself of the whole body of previous science (analogy, cross-field clues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifold connections between sciences give clues to likely laws; out of many possible hypotheses select those most probable given existing knowledge. Historical examples: great scientists used prior theory to guide fruitful hypotheses rather than blind empiricism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional character and requirement of repeated testing
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis is provisional: even if results agree with expectations, we must proceed to further deductions and new trials rather than treat initial agreement as final proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tests conflict with expectations, modify or abandon the hypothesis. Every new fact may suggest refinements. This iterative testing is central to scientific progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undue reliance on simple proportionality (treat simple laws as provisional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple proportional relations (y = mx + n or y = m x) should be treated as provisionally true and suspected when more precise measurement or more complex interactions are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small segments of curves appear linear; early investigators often assumed proportionality when curvature was undetectable. Expect simple proportion in elementary/direct unimpeded actions, but be cautious: many apparent simple laws are approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness is a defect — suspect vague hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Vagueness and incapability of precise proof or disproof often enable false theories to survive; vagueness should excite suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothesis that cannot be rendered into precise consequences is harder to refute and therefore less reliable. Demand definite modes of testing; be skeptical of explanations that avoid numerical/qualitative specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher evidential burden for hypotheses conflicting with well-established beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: The more a new hypothesis conflicts with previously well-founded beliefs, the greater the evidence required in its favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no law is proved with absolute certainty, new hypotheses can displace old ones; however, the probability assigned to the old hypothesis dictates how much stronger the confirming evidence for the new must be before acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses may be inconceivable yet acceptable if they conform to facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty of conception (inconceivable magnitude or counterintuitive properties) is not by itself a reason to reject a hypothesis provided it is not self-contradictory and it accords with observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gravity acting instantaneously or ether being 'absolutely solid' are hard to conceive but accepted because they explain observed phenomena. Do not discard theories solely because they defy ordinary intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage of hypothesis and experiment (methodological principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive investigation consists in the marriage of hypothesis and experiment: frame hypotheses from facts, deduce consequences, and verify by new facts/experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory should lead to selection of the most critical experiments. Blind accumulation of facts (pure empiricism) is inadequate for complex subjects; hypothesis-driven selection increases efficiency and discovery.
